en: The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*: An Easy Explanation.
Sages establish worldly dharmas to maintain social customs and moral transformation. Our Buddha teaches supramundane dharmas to guide the deluded masses.
Both the mundane and the supramundane ultimately converge upon goodness. However, worldly dharmas do not transcend the daily conduct of human relations.
The supramundane Dharma is that which can transform the ordinary into the holy; it is the most excellent among all that is good.
The Heart Sutra is the very essence of Prajñāpāramitā and the shortcut to the supramundane. By practicing in reliance upon this, one is able to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.

Is this not the Sublime Dharma? Now that this *Easy Explanation Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* has been completed, I have accordingly categorized and annotated this scripture alongside it.

It is my hope that these works may provide mutual benefit, thereby establishing the causal conditions for transcending the world. May all who see or hear them together ascend the path to enlightenment. At this time...
Written by Xie Chengmu, Guansan, at the Hunlao Hermitage in the late spring of the Jichou year of the Guangxu era.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty: The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Annotated by Xie Chengmu of Piling, member of the Guansan clan;
published by Liu Shaonan of Yuanjue, Zhenzhou;
and proofread by Jiang Chuntong of Lanyan.
Published by Qian Songling Juezhi:
This sutra takes single dharmas as its name, true reality (*tathatā*) as its essence, contemplative observation as its school, and the deliverance from suffering as its function.
The Mahāyāna constitutes the doctrinal characteristics. These five points are all the essential purports explained within the sūtras.

"Single Dharma" refers to the Prajñāpāramitā. "True Reality" refers to the empty nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*). "Contemplative Observation" refers to the clear vision that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are all empty.
"Delivering from Suffering" refers to delivering [beings] from all suffering and calamity. "Mahāyāna" refers to Bodhi...
This is the profound *prajñā* practiced by the Bodhisattva. The title of the sutra refers to *prajñā*, which in the language of China means "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*).
*Pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore" (*dàobītàn*). Sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding the nature of wisdom, dwell in birth and death; this is called "this shore."
By cultivating prajñā, the bodhisattva awakens to the nature of wisdom and reaches nirvāṇa, which is called the "other shore.
"Mind" refers to the mind of prajñā. This prajñā-mind is inherently possessed by every person; this sutra is taught so that they may perceive their original nature.
"Sutra" means "constant" and "dharma."
According to the translation by Shi Hu: The World-Honored One was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, having entered the samādhi called "Proclaiming the True Dharma through Profound Radiance.

Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "If there be anyone who wishes to practice and study this profound gateway of the Prajñāpāramitā, how should they practice and study it? The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
He then preached this sutra, which is the essential distillation of the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* spoken by the World-Honored One.
It has been transmitted to China in five translations; the present version follows that translated by Xuanzang, as it is the one most widely circulated in the Middle Kingdom.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he [perceived that] all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered himself from all suffering and distress.
[Note on Pronunciation]: "Xing" (行) is pronounced *han*; "Banruo" (般若) is pronounced *bo-re*. [Commentary]: "Avalokiteśvara" is the same as Guanshiyin (觀世音).
Because he employs the wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate and realize the purity of his own mind—perfectly integrated and unimpeded—he is called "Zizai" (Sovereign Master).
It is said that when a bodhisattva, practicing the profound path of their own way and mounting the wisdom of prajñā,
reaches the further shore of nirvāṇa,
they perceive that the five aggregates are all empty and transcend all suffering and calamity.

"Shines upon" means contemplative observation. "The five aggregates" (pañcaskandha) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Aggregate" (skandha) means accumulation. "Form" (rūpa) refers to the physical body.

"Sensation" (vedanā) means experiencing and receiving. "Perception" (saṃjñā) means conceptualization and thought. "Mental formations" (saṃskāra) mean volitional activity and creation. "Consciousness" (vijñāna) means discernment and differentiation.

Because there is a physical body, there arise feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "To cross over" means to be liberated from all suffering and distress—the manifold sufferings of the world.
This refers to the Bodhisattva, through the power of contemplative observation, perceiving the aforementioned five aggregates.
All are empty and non-existent. It is by means of this that one delivers the world from all its sufferings.
The above are the words of the compilers of the sūtras, Śāriputra.
This refers to Śāriputra, a disciple of the Buddha who was foremost in wisdom.
Because he had requested this on behalf of the assembly, the Bodhisattva called him by name and addressed him. From this point until the end, these are the words of Avalokiteśvara.
Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Form refers to all phenomenal appearances in the world, which are entirely illusory and false. Emptiness is true emptiness, forever free from decay or extinction.
While it is certainly true that the illusory forms of the world are empty and false, one need not give rise to a mind of revulsion or detachment toward them. This is the truth.
Emptiness should indeed be cultivated, yet one need not give rise to a mind of grasping or attachment. If conceptual discrimination arises, both become afflictions.
One should know that illusory form is not different from true emptiness, and true emptiness is not different from illusory form;

one must not discriminate between what to accept or reject. Furthermore, illusory form is itself true emptiness, and true emptiness is itself illusory form; it is essential to understand it in this way.
To realize this is precisely the right path.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. [Note:
"Fù" (復) is pronounced with the departing tone. Now, if one does not give rise to discrimination between form and emptiness, then feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
It is likewise so for all else. From "Form is not different from emptiness" up to this point constitutes the essential core of practice.
Śāriputra, this mark of the emptiness of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases.
*xiàng* (pronounced with the departing tone). ○ "These phenomena" refers to the aforementioned five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"The characteristic of emptiness" refers to the true characteristic of ultimate emptiness. The Bodhisattva again addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"If one can thoroughly understand that the phenomena of the five aggregates are themselves the true characteristic of ultimate emptiness, then the essence of this true characteristic is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Since there is no arising..."
It is extinguished. How could there be defilement or purity? Since there is neither defilement nor purity, how could there be increase or decrease?
Therefore, within emptiness, there is no form; there is no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Within the true mark of ultimate emptiness, since there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor defilement nor purity, nor increase nor decrease, there are likewise no five aggregates to be known.
There are no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena are called the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
For example, because form is seen by means of the eye, the eye is the faculty and form is the object. Such are the six faculties and the six objects.

Taken together, these constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*). It is said that within true emptiness, since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) do not exist, the sense faculties and their objects must likewise not exist.
The absence of faculties and objects constitutes the emptiness of the twelve bases.
There is no eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), and so forth, up to no mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
These constitute the six consciousnesses, namely: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, each having its own consciousness.

As for "element" (*dhātu*), it refers to the range from the point where the eye sees to the point where it does not see. The phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*) indicates the beginning and the end while omitting the middle.

These six consciousnesses, combined with the aforementioned twelve bases (*āyatana*), constitute the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Regarding these three categories of faculties, objects, and consciousness, one can realize and enter [the truth] by practicing according to any single category.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; likewise, there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.

This is called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), also known as the twelve factors of existence (*dvādaśabhava-aṅga*). The first is ignorance (*avidyā*), also termed affliction (*kleśa*).
The second is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to the performance of various karmic actions. These two links pertain to what was done in past lives.
...the cause thereof. Third is consciousness (*vijñāna*): this refers to the arising of deluded thoughts when first taking recourse in the mother’s womb. Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):

from the time after taking recourse in the womb, the various sense faculties and mental formations arise. Fifth is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): these are formed within the womb as the six faculties. Sixth is contact (*sparśa*):
after emerging from the womb, the six faculties encounter the six sense objects. Seventh is sensation (*vedanā*): this refers to experiencing...
The inclusion of worldly matters such as the pleasant and the unpleasant constitutes these five links; they are the fruits experienced in the present life.

Eighth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which refers to the defiled attachment to the five objects of desire. Ninth is grasping (*upādāna*), which refers to the arising of a mind of clinging toward various objects.
Tenth is becoming (*bhava*), which refers to creating the causes of outflow (*sāsrava*) that can summon the fruits of the future. This...
The three links constitute the causes produced in the present life. The eleventh is birth (*jāti*), which refers to receiving a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the future.
The twelfth is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which refers to that future body having both aged and died.
These two links are the fruits to be experienced in future lives. These twelve links of dependent origination encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time;
they depend upon one another in succession like the rotation of a wheel, without ceasing. That sentient beings are deluded and do not awaken is truly pitiable.
For "ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to the darkness of folly; it means being devoid of clarity regarding one's own fundamental nature.
"Thoroughly understood" does not mean a state of dullness or ignorance; rather, it refers to a realization that is contrary to [deluded] reasoning.

"There is no ignorance" means that by means of the wisdom of *prajñā*, one contemplates this ignorance and sees that its nature is fundamentally empty, devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
hence it is said, "there is no ignorance. Likewise, there is "no end to ignorance. This principle extends even to "no old age and death, and no end to old age and death."
It is the same as before; it cites the beginning and the end while encompassing that which lies between them.

There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path—these constitute the Four Noble Truths. Suffering refers to the fruit of suffering within birth and death; the origin refers to the causes of suffering, namely afflictions and karma. These two—

These are the phenomena of the mundane world. Cessation (*nirodha*) is the blissful fruit of *nirvāṇa*, and the Path (*mārga*) is the blissful cause consisting of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

These two are the supramundane phenomena. By teaching these Four Noble Truths, one intends to cause sentient beings to know suffering, abandon its origin, aspire toward cessation, and cultivate the path, thereby leaving suffering behind and attaining bliss.
When a Bodhisattva illuminates and realizes this realm, they see that its very substance is empty and quiescent; therefore—
It is also said that there is "non-existence.
There is neither wisdom nor attainment.
From the five aggregates up to the four noble truths, one thoroughly understands that they all lack any mark of true reality; this is truly due to *prajñā*.
Only through the power of wisdom and contemplative insight can one reach this state.

However, if you perceive that you possess this wisdom and are able to empty all objective realms, you will have a sense of attainment regarding the Way. If such a view persists, it will immediately obstruct the Way.
Therefore it is said: "There is neither wisdom nor attainment. When one's practice reaches this point, both person and phenomena are empty, and both object and wisdom are extinguished;
it is like when the illness has departed, the medicine is forgotten.
"Because there is nothing to be apprehended.
This phrase serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.
"The Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind."

"Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is abbreviated as "Pusa. Regarding the title of the sutra, *Prajñāpāramitā*, it means that when a bodhisattva practices according to this Dharma of *prajñāpāramitā*, the essence of the mind becomes perfectly luminous and naturally free of deluded thoughts.
When deluded thoughts do not arise, what hindrance could there be for the mind?
Ah! Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate nirvana.
When the mind of a Bodhisattva is free from hindrance, they naturally have no alarm, fear, or dread. Since there is no fear...
When fear ceases, all inverted delusions and false imaginings likewise do not arise; this constitutes the emptiness of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*).
Yet, delusion is itself the three obstacles, while awakening is itself the three virtues (*tridharma*); that is to say, afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves bodhi.

Therefore, one ultimately reaches the ground of nirvāṇa, where even the name of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) no longer exists. This would not be possible were it not for the contemplative observation of *prajñā*.
How could [worldly] merit ever equal this? It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the brilliance appears.
Because the Buddhas of the three periods rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The "three periods of time" refers to the past, present, and future. As for the aforementioned dharmas, it is not only Bodhisattvas who rely upon them for cultivation and realization;
even the Buddhas of the three periods have all attained perfect enlightenment by means of these very same principles.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; in the language of the flowers [Sanskrit], it means "Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Right Enlightenment.
Therefore, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, and an unsurpassed mantra.
This is the peerless mantra.

Therefore, one should know that the True Dharma of Prajñā consists of four kinds of mantras. Because the function of Prajñā can destroy demonic obstacles, it is called the Great Divine Mantra (*mahā-vidyā-mantra*).
Because it can extinguish the darkness of ignorance, it is called the Great Illuminating Mantra (*mahā-jñāna-mantra*). Because it can manifest the ultimate...
This principle is called the Unsurpassed Mantra; as the fruit of supreme, wondrous enlightenment, it has no equal and is thus called the Peerless Mantra.

"Mantra" refers to esoteric speech; by upholding it, one obtains benefits according to one's wishes. It is said that the merit of this Prajñā encompasses both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, truly constituting a most excellent gateway to the True Dharma.
"It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.

To say that the efficacy of Prajñā is vast and great, and that by following and practicing it one will certainly eliminate suffering and attain happiness—this leaves no room for doubt and inspires faith in people.
Therefore, the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken. It is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. The above constitutes the explicit teaching of the Prajñā;
this [mantra] is the implicit teaching. For a mantra is the secret language of the Buddha. It is not...
This is something known only by the Buddhas; therefore, it has not been translated. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "A mantra is the name of a king of ghosts.
By invoking the name of the king, the tribes will respect their lord; thus, one is able to subdue all malevolent spirits.
Furthermore, a mantra is like a secret password within an army: when the password is called out and corresponds [to the other], there is no [need for further explanation].

Regarding "that which is invoked" (*sokaman*): furthermore, "mantra" (*dhāraṇī*) means a vow (*praṇidhāna*). It is like the *gonglo* wasp’s incantation toward the *mingling* caterpillar, wishing that it become like itself.
When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak mantras, they wish that all sentient beings may all, like themselves, attain the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
If one is able to recite this mantra, then whatever one vows for shall be accomplished without exception.
The Divine Mantra for Rebirth in the Pure Land: Namo Amitābhāya. Tathāgatāya. Tadyathā. Amitiṭu.

*Bhāvi amṛtaḥ, stambhāvi amṛtaḥ, vikaraṇe amṛtaḥ, vikaraṇḍa, gamini, gagana, jitakāle svāhā.* If one recites this sūtra as an offering for the deceased and also recites this mantra, they will immediately attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Its spiritual efficacy is extraordinary. Attached.
Recorded here for the purpose of practice and application.
